procedural_history.originating_court: Court of Sessions, East Thanjavur Division at Nagapattinam
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 4.8.1972 of the Madras High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 23 of 1971
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused persons appealed the conviction to the High Court of Judicature at Madras in Criminal Appeal No. 23 of 1971. The High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the conviction and sentences passed by the Court of Sessions.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused persons approached the Supreme Court by way of a special leave petition under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, challenging the High Court's judgment and order.

issue.issue_text: Under what circumstances will the Supreme Court, in its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, interfere with a conviction and sentence that have been concurrently upheld by the trial and appellate courts?

facts: The accused were convicted and sentenced by a trial court.
This conviction and sentence were upheld by an appellate court, resulting in a concurrent finding of guilt.
The conviction was based on eyewitness testimony that the lower courts found proved the charges beyond a reasonable doubt.
law: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court will not grant special leave to appeal unless exceptional and special circumstances exist.
Interference is warranted only if substantial and grave injustice has been done and the case has features of sufficient gravity.
The Court does not act as a third court to re-review evidence.
An exception is made if a lower court's failure to apprehend the true effect of material evidence results in a failure of justice.
Specifically regarding a sentence, the Court will not interfere unless there is an illegality or it involves a question of principle.
application: The Court examined the concurrent findings of the lower courts.
It found that the conviction was properly based on eyewitness evidence that two courts had already deemed credible.
The Court concluded that there was no "infirmity far less any illegality or failure of justice" in the conviction.
Similarly, it found no illegality or question of principle involved in the sentencing that would justify its interference.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it will only interfere with a conviction and sentence concurrently upheld by lower courts in exceptional circumstances where there is a grave injustice, an illegality, or a failure of justice. Since none of these conditions were met in this case, the Court refused to interfere and dismissed the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Under what circumstances will the Supreme Court, in its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, interfere with a conviction and sentence that have been concurrently upheld by the trial and appellate courts?
appellant_arguments: The Supreme Court should interfere in this case because the lower courts failed to apprehend the true effect of a material change in the versions given by witnesses between their initial statements and their trial testimony, leading to a failure of justice.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not interfere with the concurrent findings of the lower courts, as it does not convert itself into a third court to review evidence.

The conviction was correctly based on eyewitness testimony that proved the charges beyond a reasonable doubt, and there was no illegality, infirmity, or failure of justice in the lower courts' decisions.

cases.principle: The Supreme Court does not grant special leave to appeal under Article 136(1) to review evidence for a third time, but will interfere if the lower court fails to apprehend the true effect of a material change in witness testimony which results in a failure of justice.

cases.case_name: Sadlu Singh Barnam Singh v. State of Pepsu
cases.principle: Cited as a case that followed and relied upon the decision in Pritam Singh v. The State regarding the Supreme Court's exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 136(1).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court will not grant special leave to appeal under Article 136(1) of the Constitution, nor convert itself into a third court to review evidence, unless it is shown that exceptional and special circumstances exist, that substantial and grave injustice has been done, and the case presents features of sufficient gravity to warrant a review of the decision appealed against. An interference may be warranted if the lower court fails to apprehend the true effect of a material change in witness testimony, resulting in a failure of justice.
obiter: Only those points can be urged at the final hearing of the appeal which are fit to be urged at the preliminary stage when leave is asked for.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found no infirmity, illegality, or failure of justice in the concurrent decisions of the lower courts that would warrant interference with the conviction and sentence, as the charges were proven by eyewitness testimony beyond a reasonable doubt and the sentence involved no illegality or question of principle.
legal_tests_applied: The Supreme Court will interfere with a conviction and sentence only when it is "shown that exceptional and special circumstances exist, that substantial and grave injustice has been done and the case in question presents features of sufficient gravity to warrant a review of the decision appealed against."
The Supreme Court "does not by special leave convert itself into a court to review evidence of a third time."

An exception to the non-interference rule exists where "the court below fails in apprehending the true effect of a material change in the versions given by the witnesses... when it occasions a failure of justice."
The Supreme Court "would not interfere with the sentence passed by the Courts below unless there is an illegality in it or the same involves any question of principle."
why_appellant_lost: The Court found no "infirmity for less any illegality or failure of justice which would impel us to interfere with the order of conviction and sentence concurrently arrived at by both the courts below."

The Court was satisfied that the conviction was correctly based on evidence, stating that "the accused 1 and 2 have been convicted by the courts below on the finding that the offences charged against them have been proved by the eye witnesses beyond any reasonable doubt."
The Court found no grounds to interfere with the sentence, as there was "no illegality nor any question of principle involved in the matter of making order sentencing them to imprisonment."
why_respondent_won: The Court adhered to its established principle that it "does not by special leave convert itself into a court to review evidence of a third time."
The Court accepted the lower courts' findings that the charges were proven by eyewitnesses beyond a reasonable doubt, thereby validating the conviction.
The Court found no illegality or principled error in the sentence, thus upholding the concurrent decisions of the lower courts.
policy_considerations: The Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 is discretionary and not intended to create a third tier of routine evidence review, thereby preserving the finality of decisions from lower appellate courts.

The Court's intervention in cases of concurrent findings is reserved for exceptional circumstances to correct a substantial and grave injustice, ensuring the integrity of the judicial process without becoming a regular court of appeal.
